## BLOG: What Is a Search Fund? A Beginner's Guide to Buying a Business With Other People's Money

URL: https://www.kautilya-pe.com/blog/what-is-a-search-fund
Author: Dev Shah · Published: 28 July 2026 · 9 min read

A search fund is an investment vehicle through which investors pay an entrepreneur to spend about
two years finding a private company to buy, then fund the purchase and hand that entrepreneur the
CEO seat. The model was conceived at Stanford Graduate School of Business in 1984.

In plain terms: you do not need to be rich to buy a business. You need to be credible enough that
other people will fund your search, and then fund your acquisition. That is the entire idea.

This guide covers how the model works, where the money comes from at each stage, what the
entrepreneur actually earns, what kind of company gets bought, and where the model does not fit.
No prior finance background assumed.

### The Problem a Search Fund Solves

Most people who want to run a company can either start one or buy one, and both routes have an
obvious blocker.

- Starting one means years of no revenue, no customers, and a high failure rate before you find
  out whether it works.
- Buying one means writing a cheque for a profitable business, which usually costs several million
  dollars. Most capable operators in their late twenties or thirties do not have that.

The search fund is the workaround. It splits the problem into two separate fundraises:

- First, raise a small amount to fund the search itself. Enough to pay yourself a modest salary
  while you look, full time, for a company worth buying.
- Then, raise the much larger amount to actually buy the business, once you have found a specific
  target with real numbers attached.

The insight is that investors will not hand an unproven operator millions of dollars up front.
They will, however, fund a two-year search cheaply, then decide deal by deal whether to fund the
purchase. The searcher is buying credibility in instalments.

This is why the model sits inside the broader idea of entrepreneurship through acquisition (often
shortened to ETA): becoming an entrepreneur by buying an existing business rather than founding one.

### How a Search Fund Works, Stage by Stage

Four stages, running roughly four to seven years end to end.

- Stage 1: Raise the search capital. The searcher raises a small fund from a group of investors,
  typically six to ten experienced search fund backers, to pay salary, travel and admin while they
  look for a company.
- Stage 2: Search. The searcher spends roughly two years contacting owners, screening companies,
  and negotiating. Median time to acquisition is about 20 months, per Stanford data.
- Stage 3: Acquire. Once a target is agreed, the searcher returns to the same investors to fund the
  purchase. They have first claim on the deal, but no obligation. Debt usually covers part of the
  price.
- Stage 4: Operate, then exit. The searcher becomes CEO and runs the company, typically for five to
  seven years, growing profits before selling. The biggest payday comes at exit, not at
  acquisition.

### Where the Money Comes From

Search funds raise capital twice, on very different terms. This two-step structure is the defining
feature of the model.

| | Search Capital | Acquisition Capital |
|---|---|---|
| When | Before any target is identified | Once a specific company is agreed |
| Typical size | ~$400,000–500,000 (~₹3.9–4.8 crore) | $6M–24M equity (~₹58–232 crore) |
| What it buys | ~24 months of salary, travel, admin | The company itself |
| Who provides it | 6–10 search fund investors | Usually the same investors, plus debt |
| Risk | Very high — many searches never close a deal | Lower — a real business with real numbers |

Two mechanics matter and are easy to miss:

- The step-up. Money put into the search converts into acquisition equity at a premium,
  industry-standard 1.5x. Invest $100,000 (~₹96.6 lakh) in the search, and it counts as $150,000
  (~₹1.45 crore) of equity at the acquisition. This compensates investors for backing a person with
  no target yet.
- Right of first refusal. Search investors get the pro-rata right of first refusal on the
  acquisition equity. They can fund the deal on the same terms as anyone else, before outside money
  is invited. It is a right, not an obligation, so a weak target can still fail to attract funding.

Total deal sizes typically run $10M to $30M (~₹97 crore to ~₹290 crore), with bank or seller debt
covering 20% to 40% of the purchase price.

### What the Searcher Actually Earns

Median searcher equity at acquisition is 25%, rising to 30–35% if performance targets are met. But
that equity is not handed over at closing. It vests in three roughly equal tranches:

| Tranche | Vests When | What It Rewards |
|---|---|---|
| First third | At closing of the acquisition | Finding and completing a deal |
| Second third | Over the following 4–5 years | Staying and operating the business |
| Final third | At exit, based on IRR achieved | Actually generating returns |

The third tranche is tied to the internal rate of return delivered to investors at exit: below 20%
IRR delivered to investors, the searcher earns nothing from the final tranche; between 20% and 35%
it vests on a sliding scale; at 35% or above the searcher receives the full tranche.

A searcher who buys a company, runs it competently for six years, and returns 15% a year to
investors keeps roughly two thirds of their equity and forfeits the rest. The model does not pay
for effort. It pays for outcome.

### What a Search Fund Actually Buys

The target profile is narrow, and deliberately boring. Investors are funding a first-time CEO, so
they want a business that will not punish inexperience.

| Criterion | Typical Requirement |
|---|---|
| EBITDA (annual operating profit) | Above $2M (~₹19.3 crore), ideally $2–4M (~₹19–39 crore) |
| EBITDA margin | Above 15% |
| Recurring revenue | 60%+ under contract |
| Business model | Services, B2B or B2C, simple operations |
| Capital expenditure | Low maintenance capex |
| Industry growth | At least 2x GDP growth |
| Track record | Consistent history of profit |

The pattern: predictable cash flow, low capital intensity, and no technological cliff edge. A
profitable, unglamorous, contract-heavy services business is close to the ideal. High-growth
startups, capital-hungry manufacturers, and anything requiring deep technical specialisation are
typically avoided.

### Two Main Variants

- Traditional (funded) search. Investors fund the search, get the step-up and the right of first
  refusal, and the searcher takes a salary while looking. Lower personal financial risk, less
  control, smaller equity share.
- Self-funded search. The searcher funds their own search, usually while working, and finances the
  acquisition with debt and seller financing rather than a syndicate of institutional backers.
  Higher personal risk and no salary during the search, but a substantially larger equity stake and
  no investor group to answer to. Self-funded searchers typically buy smaller companies than the
  $10M–$30M range above.

Accelerator-backed and sponsor-backed variants also exist, where an institution provides
infrastructure and support alongside capital.

### Where the Model Does Not Fit

- Many searches never close. The search capital is genuinely at risk, and a meaningful share of
  searchers finish two years without an acquisition.
- You are buying a job you cannot easily quit. The second vesting tranche runs four to five years.
  Leaving early forfeits equity.
- The performance hurdle is demanding. A 20% IRR floor before the final tranche pays anything is a
  high bar for a small services business in a slow-growing sector.
- The target profile excludes most businesses. EBITDA above $2M with 60% recurring revenue rules
  out the overwhelming majority of small companies.
- It is heavily concentrated in the US and Canada. The Stanford study that defines the model's
  track record covers funds formed in those two markets.

### What This Looks Like Outside the US

The classic search fund targets deals of $10M to $30M. A large share of real acquisition activity
in India and other emerging markets happens well below that. Kautilya's own published engagements
illustrate the spread: one confidential managed-services deal ($21M) sits inside the classic range;
others (SmartPrompt $12K, Dino Games $39K, Runify $110K, Inspire3 $1.8M) sit far below it.

Three practical consequences follow (Kautilya's read, not published data — no equivalent India
dataset exists):

- The search capital stage is often skipped. At a $100,000 purchase price, raising a $450,000
  search fund to find it makes no sense.
- Self-funded search is the more realistic template for most first-time acquirers in these markets.
- The screening discipline still transfers even when the structure does not: recurring revenue, low
  capex, boring and profitable, no technology cliff.

The structure is US-shaped. The diligence logic is universal.

### FAQ

**What is a search fund?** An investment vehicle, conceived in 1984 at Stanford Graduate School of
Business, through which investors financially support an entrepreneur's efforts to locate, acquire,
manage and grow a privately held company. The entrepreneur raises a small fund to finance a roughly
two-year search, then raises a larger amount from the same investors to buy the company they find,
and becomes its CEO.

**How does a search fund work?** In four stages: raise search capital from six to ten investors;
spend about 20 months finding a company; return to those investors to fund the acquisition, usually
alongside debt; then run the business as CEO for five to seven years before selling.

**How much money do you need to start a search fund?** Typically none of your own for a traditional
search. Investors provide roughly $400,000 to $500,000 of search capital covering about 24 months
of salary and expenses. A self-funded search reverses this.

**How much equity does a searcher get?** Median equity at acquisition is 25%, rising to 30–35% if
performance targets are met, vesting in three tranches (closing, 4–5 years of operating, and exit
tied to IRR). Below 20% IRR the final tranche pays nothing.

**What kind of business does a search fund buy?** Profitable, unglamorous companies with EBITDA
above $2M, margins above 15%, 60%+ recurring revenue, simple operations, low capex, and industry
growth at least 2x GDP.

**What is entrepreneurship through acquisition?** The broader idea of becoming an entrepreneur by
buying an existing business rather than founding one. A search fund is the most formalised version.

**Do search funds exist in India?** The formal model is concentrated in the US and Canada. Real
acquisition activity in India often happens at deal sizes below the classic search fund range,
where self-funded structures fit better.

Sources: Stanford GSB Center for Entrepreneurial Studies (Search Funds, 2026 Search Fund Study);
Pacific Lake Partners (Intro to Search Funds); Acquisition Stars and Search Funds News (investor
agreements, searcher economics); IESE Business School and Yale SOM (academic context). Not
investment advice.

## BLOG: Buying a Family-Owned Business in India: What First-Time Buyers Need to Know

URL: https://www.kautilya-pe.com/blog/buying-family-owned-business-india
Author: Dev Shah · Published: 25 July 2026 · 7 min read

Most small businesses for sale in India are family businesses. A promoter built it over 15 or 25
years, ran it with relatives or long-time loyal staff, and is now selling because of retirement,
health, or the next generation choosing a different career. This is a different transaction from
buying a professionally-run, systemized company, with its own specific risks and negotiation
dynamics that generic due diligence advice doesn't fully cover.

### Why Buying a Family-Owned Business in India Is Different

A professionally-run business sale is largely a numbers exercise: verify the financials, agree a
price, transfer ownership. A family business sale carries an additional layer, because the business
and the owner's identity are often the same thing. Three structural differences show up
consistently.

### 1. Informal Financial Records in Family-Owned Businesses

Family businesses, especially those run for a decade or more without professional management,
frequently keep looser financial records than the business's actual revenue would suggest:

- Cash transactions not fully reflected in books, sometimes to reduce tax exposure, sometimes just
  from years of informal habit.
- Owner expenses mixed with business expenses: a family car, personal travel, or relatives on
  payroll doing minimal actual work.
- Multiple sets of numbers: what's reported for tax, what's shown to a bank for a loan, and what
  the owner tells you privately may all differ.

None of this necessarily means fraud. It often means the business has been run the way a family
managed it for 20 years, not the way a buyer needs it documented. Expect to spend more time
normalizing financials than with a corporatized target.

### 2. Employee Loyalty in Family Business Acquisitions

In a family business, key employees are frequently loyal to the promoter personally — sometimes
because they're relatives, sometimes because of decades-long personal relationships. This creates a
retention risk that doesn't show up in a standard organizational chart review. Questions worth
asking before you close: which employees are related to the seller and do they intend to stay?
Does the business depend on informal knowledge the owner holds in their head, or relationships built
on personal trust? Will long-serving staff accept a new, unrelated owner?

### 3. Negotiating With a Family Business Owner in India

Negotiating with a founder who built the business is different from negotiating with a private
equity seller or a corporate divestiture team:

- Attachment to a number that isn't grounded in financials — the owner may have a price in mind
  tied to what the business means to them, not what it earns.
- Sensitivity around legacy and continuity — many family sellers care more than a corporate seller
  would about whether the business, brand name, or staff will be treated well after the sale.
- Slower decision timelines, particularly when multiple family members need to agree.

Sellers motivated by continuity and legacy, rather than purely maximizing price, are often more open
to structures like seller financing, transition consulting periods, or earnouts.

### Family Business Succession Due Diligence Checklist

- Family employment audit: list every employee related to the seller, their actual role and
  output, and whether they're staying post-sale.
- Verbal agreement inventory: identify supplier terms, customer arrangements, or informal
  understandings that were never written down.
- Owner dependency mapping: determine which functions only the owner can perform, and build a
  realistic transition timeline.
- Multiple financial record reconciliation: compare tax filings, bank statements, and any informal
  figures the seller shares privately.
- Family agreement confirmation: verify all owners (siblings, spouse, adult children with a stake)
  are actually aligned on the sale.

### How to Structure an Acquisition of a Family-Owned Business

- A transition consulting period, where the seller stays on for 3 to 6 months post-sale to hand
  over supplier and customer relationships personally.
- Seller financing or an earnout tied to retained customers.
- Written retention agreements with key family or long-serving employees, signed before closing.

The goal is converting informal, personal trust into documented, transferable business relationships
before you take ownership.

### Red Flags When Buying a Family-Owned Business

- Reluctance to share full financial records early, when it stems from decades of informal
  bookkeeping rather than active concealment.
- A seller who wants to remain heavily involved post-sale in a way that suggests they haven't
  actually decided to exit.
- Key relatives or staff who are notably absent from negotiations but clearly influential in daily
  operations.

None of these mean walk away. They mean slow down, ask directly, and structure the deal to account
for what you find.

### FAQ

**Is buying a family-owned business riskier than buying a corporate-run one?** Not inherently
riskier, but the risks are different in kind. Financial informality and owner/employee dependency
need more attention; outright fraud or complex corporate liabilities are often less of a factor.

**How do I value a family business with informal financial records?** Start by reconciling all
available records — bank statements, tax filings, GST returns — against what the seller states
verbally. A CA experienced in SME valuations can normalize the numbers, but expect the process to
take longer.

**Will employees stay after a family business is sold to an unrelated buyer?** It depends heavily
on how the transition is handled. Direct conversations with key staff before closing, retention
agreements for critical roles, and a visible transition period all improve the odds.

**Should I be concerned if a family business seller wants to stay on after the sale?** Not
necessarily. A defined transition period is often valuable. The concern is a seller who wants to
stay indefinitely involved, which usually signals they haven't committed to the exit.

## NEWSLETTER: How to Value a Founder-Owned Pharma Business in India

URL: https://www.kautilya-pe.com/newsletter/torrent-jb-chemicals-pharma-valuation
Author: Dev Shah · Published: 29 June 2025 · 12 min read
Key metrics: ₹3,100 Cr KKR entry (2020) → ₹25,689 Cr Torrent exit (2025), 8x return in 5 years.

If you run a pharma business in India and have not read the Torrent-JB Chemicals deal announcement
carefully, you should. Not because it is a pharma story. Because it is the clearest public data
point in years on what your business is actually worth — and what it would be worth if you spent
five years preparing it properly before a sale.

Torrent Pharmaceuticals paid 24.8× EBITDA for JB Chemicals in June 2025. KKR had bought the same
business in 2020 for roughly Rs. 3,100 Cr. Five years. Eight times the entry price. No new drugs
invented. No new markets entered. No company rebuilt from scratch.

This is a business preparation story, and the gap it reveals between what founder-owned pharma
businesses sell for today and what they could sell for with the right preparation is the most
important number in Indian mid-market M&A right now.

### What Pharma Business Valuation in India Actually Looks Like

- Founder-owned, underprepared: 6–8× EBITDA
- PE-backed, institutional: 18–24× EBITDA
- JB Chemicals 2025 (Torrent deal): 24.8×

The current market prices founder-owned pharma businesses in the Rs. 50 to 500 Cr revenue range at
6 to 8× EBITDA. PE-backed assets with institutional governance and professional management trade at
18 to 24×. That is not a sector difference — both pools sit in the same therapeutic categories, same
geographies, same regulatory environment. The difference is diligence-readiness.

JB Chemicals under the Mody family: Rs. 2,800 Cr revenue, EBITDA margins of 15–18%. Under KKR: 18%
revenue CAGR, margins of 27–29%, Rs. 7–7.5 billion in annual free cash flow. Same assets. Different
preparation. Three times the multiple.

### Five Decisions That Created Rs. 22,000 Crore of Exit Value

1. **Separate ownership from management on day one.** KKR appointed Nikhil Chopra as CEO within
   weeks — a 24-year Cipla veteran. The Mody family exited operations immediately and cleanly. An
   acquirer will not pay 20× for a business that stops working when the promoter steps back.
2. **Run a consistent bolt-on acquisition strategy.** Five bolt-on acquisitions in four years, each
   receiving the same operating playbook. Sporlac grew 34% post-acquisition. Razel grew 33%. JB
   Chemicals moved from 28th to 21st in the Indian pharma market.
3. **Fund the capability the promoter had been ignoring.** The CDMO arm — medicated lozenges with
   global potential — was 11% of revenue when KKR arrived, starved of capital. By FY25 it generated
   Rs. 446 Cr annually with global leadership in a USD 4.6 billion segment.
4. **Improve the economics without changing the business.** EBITDA margins nearly doubled — from
   15–18% to a guided 27–29% — through supply chain optimisation and product mix discipline, not
   price increases.
5. **Build governance so any buyer can understand the business quickly.** An institutional board,
   credentialed independent directors, and an audit trail rebuilt to diligence standards. When
   Torrent arrived at the data room, there were no structural surprises.

### Why the Next 24 Months Are an Unusual Window

- **Schedule M**: Revised Schedule M became binding on January 1, 2026. Tier 3 manufacturers who
  cannot fund the upgrades are approaching advisors now — not distressed, but unable to wait out
  another market cycle.
- **PE Capital**: ChrysCapital's Rs. 1,300 Cr acquisition of 71% of Novartis India in Q1 2026
  confirmed institutional buyers are not on the sidelines. The Torrent-JB deal sets the ceiling
  multiple.
- **Succession**: Second-generation families across the Rs. 50–300 Cr pharma segment are facing a
  question the first generation never had to answer: does this business need to stay in the family?

### What a Valuation-Ready Pharma Business Looks Like

Governance & Documentation: at least one credentialed independent director before any formal
process; clean separation of company vs. promoter personal expenses in the P&L; all key customer
and distributor relationships documented and transferable; regulatory compliance current and
auditable (GMP, Schedule M, GST/ITR/EPF/ESI); three years of audited financials with no unexplained
adjustments; EBITDA reconciliation a buyer's CFO can verify without the promoter.

Management & Strategy: a second layer that can run the business without the promoter for 90 days;
customer concentration quantified (top five customers, contract terms, renewal history); one
identified dormant capability with a documented investment thesis; a clear answer to why a strategic
buyer would pay more than a financial buyer.

None of this requires hiring an investment bank today. It requires 12 to 24 months of deliberate
preparation.

### The Risks This Deal Creates

The Torrent-JB deal will cause some buyers to overpay for pharma assets on the assumption that every
founder-owned business contains hidden upside of the same type. It does not — the CDMO vertical at
JB Chemicals was genuinely underinvested, a specific set of conditions that does not exist in every
mid-market acquisition. For sellers, the risk is timing: the Schedule M compliance window and the
current PE deployment cycle are creating motivated but non-distressed seller conditions that will
not persist indefinitely.

### FAQ

**What EBITDA multiple do pharma businesses sell for in India?** Founder-owned businesses in the
Rs. 50–500 Cr range typically sell at 6–8× EBITDA. PE-backed assets with institutional governance
trade at 18–24×. The Torrent-JB Chemicals deal at 24.8× is the current ceiling.

**How long does it take to prepare a pharma business for sale in India?** Typically 18–36 months:
professional management layer, clean P&L, documented customer relationships, resolved governance
gaps, and funding any dormant capability.

**What did KKR do to increase JB Chemicals' value before selling to Torrent?** Appointed a
professional CEO, ran a consistent bolt-on strategy across five targets, funded a dormant CDMO
capability that grew to Rs. 446 Cr, improved EBITDA margins from 15–18% to 27–29%, and rebuilt
governance to institutional diligence standards.

**What is the difference between a motivated and a distressed seller in Indian pharma M&A?** A
motivated seller approaches the market by choice, with time and options. A distressed seller
approaches because external pressure has removed optionality. Motivated sellers price at the top of
the range; distressed sellers price at the bottom.

**Do I need an investment bank to sell a pharma business in India?** For businesses in the
Rs. 50–300 Cr range, a boutique M&A advisory firm with Indian mid-market pharma experience will
typically be more effective than a large investment bank.

## NEWSLETTER: Aurum's Housing.com Acquisition, Explained

URL: https://www.kautilya-pe.com/newsletter/aurum-housing-com-acquisition
Author: Dev Shah, Kautilya Deal Table teardown · Published: 25 July 2026 · Deal announced 16 July 2026 · 11 min read
Key metrics: ₹458 Cr deal value (all-stock) · REA's Aurum stake 5.54% → 24.90% · ~AUD 110M implied loss to REA.

REA Group "exited" Housing.com for ₹458 crore (~$47.4M), and took every rupee of it in stock, not
cash. REA's stake in the acquirer, listed proptech Aurum PropTech, jumped from 5.54% to 24.90%,
making the seller the single largest non-promoter shareholder of the company that just bought its
India business. On the reported numbers, this books REA a AUD 110 million (~$77M / ~₹744 crore)
loss. But REA didn't leave India; it rotated. Operating control of one portal traded for a quarter
of a listed acquirer.

### The Snapshot

Buyer: Aurum PropTech Ltd (BSE-listed; formerly Majesco). Target: Locon Solutions Pvt Ltd, parent of
Housing.com. Seller: REA India Pte Ltd (REA Group, Australia). Sector: Proptech / real estate
marketplaces. Size/price: ₹458.06 crore (~$47.4M), 100% share swap, zero cash. Structure: All-share
preferential issue — 1,97,93,309 Aurum shares at ₹231.42/share (~$2.40/share) to REA; REA's Aurum
stake rises 5.54% → 24.90%. Announced: July 16, 2026.

### What Happened

- July 16, 2026: Aurum PropTech's board approves acquiring 100% of Locon Solutions for ₹458.06
  crore (~$47.4M), covering equity shares, compulsorily convertible preference shares, and
  debentures on a fully diluted basis.
- The entire consideration is paid in Aurum stock: 1,97,93,309 shares issued to REA at
  ₹231.42/share (~$2.40/share), on a preferential basis. No cash changes hands.
- REA's Aurum stake rises from 5.54% to 24.90%, deliberately just under the 25% threshold that
  would trigger a mandatory open offer to Aurum's public shareholders.
- Same day, Aurum also issues 51,00,000 warrants to its own promoter at the identical ₹231.42
  price (up to ₹118 crore / ~$12.2M), taking promoter holding to 41.17% fully diluted.

Locon Solutions, founded 2012, owns Housing.com: ~58 million average monthly visits, ~12 million
monthly active users. Revenue: FY24 ₹447.49 crore (~$46.3M), FY25 ₹687.46 crore (~$71.2M, +53.7%
YoY), FY26 ₹309.93 crore (~$32.1M, unaudited) — a ~55% drop from FY25 not yet explained in public
filings. Aurum itself: ₹241.19/share (~$2.50/share) on deal day, ~₹1,738 crore (~$180M) market cap,
P/E ~96.

This is REA's second asset sold to Aurum — PropTiger went across in September 2025 for ₹86.45 crore
(~$9.0M), an all-share deal. REA entered India in January 2017 via Elara Technologies (US$50M) to
combine PropTiger and Housing.com; total investment over nine years reached roughly AUD 300 million
(~$210M / ~₹2,029 crore). Two all-share swaps, eighteen months apart, took REA from an operator with
~$210M invested to a 24.90% shareholder with zero cash recovered.

### The Numbers

Deal multiple (Kautilya estimate): ~0.67x FY25 revenue (₹458 crore deal value ÷ ₹687 crore FY25
revenue) — a 70 to 85% haircut against the 2x to 4x revenue multiples late-stage proptech rounds
fetched in 2022 to 24. That low multiple reflects three things at once: FY26 revenue softness, REA's
priority on exiting rather than maximizing price, and consideration paid in equity rather than cash.

The open question: Locon's disclosed FY26 revenue is down roughly 55% on FY25, unaudited, and the
deal's Regulation 30 annexure sizes the target on the FY25 figure, not FY26. That judgment isn't
explained in the material available; the EGM notice (August 14, 2026) may address it.

### The Structure

- Zero cash, entirely in stock. Aurum pays for a ₹458 crore acquisition, more than a quarter of its
  own ~₹1,738 crore market cap, without touching its treasury or raising new public capital.
- Priced at the regulatory floor. ₹231.42/share is the SEBI ICDR floor, about 4% below Aurum's
  deal-day close of ₹241.19.
- 24.90% is an engineered ceiling, not a coincidence. Crossing 25% would trigger a mandatory open
  offer under India's Takeover Regulations.
- A three-year lock-in. SEBI's rules on preferential allotments to non-promoters lock REA out of
  selling its new shares until roughly Q3 FY29.

Aurum's managed risk: bought scale without straining its balance sheet, avoided a cash outlay and a
public dilution event. REA's accepted risk: converted a certain, crystallized loss into an
uncertain, three-year-locked bet on Aurum's share price.

### Why It Matters

1. **REA rotated its exposure; it didn't reduce it.** Cash would have crystallized the loss and
   ended REA's India story cleanly. Instead REA holds 24.90% of the combined platform — any
   post-integration re-rating of Aurum flows back to REA. A portfolio rotation wearing the language
   of a divestment.
2. **Every listed mid-market acquirer with a credible share price now has this playbook.** The
   preferential-issue-to-one-named-allottee route is available to any listed company with stock
   investors will accept as payment.
3. **India's independent proptech portal count just dropped to three.** Housing.com and PropTiger
   now both sit under Aurum. Magicbricks belongs to Times Group; 99acres to Info Edge; NoBroker and
   a handful of smaller players remain independent.

### The Buyer's Takeaway (Advisor/Operator Lens)

1. An all-share preferential issue is a real alternative to a cash sale, not a consolation prize —
   useful for an MNC parent done running its Indian subsidiary, preserving India upside instead of
   forcing a lower-value cash exit.
2. Watch for the number just under a regulatory trigger — 24.90% next to a 25% open-offer threshold
   is an engineered ceiling, not a coincidence.
3. An unexplained revenue swing doesn't have to kill a deal, but it should change your price — it
   should show up as a lower multiple or a holdback, not get absorbed silently.

Limit: this structure depends on the buyer being listed with a share price sellers are willing to
accept as payment, and on the seller genuinely preferring optioned upside over a clean cash exit.

### The Kautilya Deal Score

Price Discipline: 4.5/5. Structure & Risk Absorption: 4.5/5. Cash-Flow Quality: 2/5. Strategic Fit /
Value Path: 4/5. Replicability: 4/5. **Overall: 3.8/5 — Solid.**

Verdict: An exceptionally well-engineered structure, cheap for the buyer, cash-preserving,
regulatorily precise, built on top of a target whose most recent year of revenue is a genuine,
unresolved red flag. The structure is the transferable lesson; the FY26 numbers are the reason this
isn't scored higher.

Sources: Aurum PropTech's BSE intimation (July 16, 2026); Business Standard, Entrackr, Business
Upturn; Screener; RP Realty Plus, Elite Agent. Currency conversions are Kautilya estimates at
approximate July 2026 spot rates (~₹96.6/$1, ~$0.70/AUD1), not independently disclosed figures.
